name: Chat System
tagline: Real-time messaging with WebSocket fan-out across many servers
summary: Clients hold a persistent WebSocket to one of many chat servers. Redis Pub/Sub fans a message out to every server that has a recipient connected, Kafka records the event durably for asynchronous consumers, and PostgreSQL stores history.

nodes.label: Browser
nodes.why: Holds one persistent WebSocket connection so the server can push messages instantly.

nodes.label: Load Balancer
nodes.why: Spreads long-lived connections across chat servers and hides individual server failures.

nodes.label: Chat Server A
nodes.why: Stateless apart from its open sockets; any number can run in parallel.

nodes.label: Chat Server B
nodes.why: A user's friends may be connected here — servers must share events.

nodes.label: Redis
nodes.why: Fast shared state: which user is on which server, and a channel every server subscribes to for fan-out.

nodes.label: Kafka
nodes.why: Messages become events that several downstream services consume independently and can replay.

nodes.label: Message Service
nodes.why: Writes messages to the database off the hot path so sending stays fast.

nodes.label: Notification Service
nodes.why: Consumes the same events to send mobile push / email when the recipient is not connected.

nodes.label: Analytics
nodes.why: A third consumer of the same stream — adding it required no change to the chat servers.

nodes.label: PostgreSQL
nodes.why: Durable, queryable store for conversations and search.

flows.name: Send a message
steps: The sender's browser pushes the message over its open WebSocket.
The load balancer routes it to the chat server that owns this connection.
Chat Server A validates it and PUBLISHes to the room channel.
Redis fans the message out to every server subscribed to that channel.
Chat Server B delivers it to recipients connected there over WebSocket.
The message is also appended to Kafka as an event.
The notification service pushes to recipients who are offline.

flows.name: Persist history
steps: Chat Server A publishes the message event.
Kafka stores it durably in the messages topic.
The message service consumes at its own pace.
History is written to PostgreSQL for search and reload.

decisions.decision: Use Redis Pub/Sub for real-time fan-out
decisions.why: Delivery to online users needs millisecond latency and every chat server must see every message for its rooms. Redis Pub/Sub is fast and simple; losing a message on a rare broker restart is acceptable because Kafka keeps the durable copy.
decisions.tradeoff: Redis Pub/Sub is fire-and-forget — no persistence, no replay. It cannot be the only path for anything that must not be lost.

decisions.decision: Use Kafka as the event log
decisions.why: History, notifications and analytics all need the same events, at different speeds, with the ability to replay after a bug fix. A durable partitioned log decouples them from the chat servers.
decisions.tradeoff: Kafka is heavy to operate. For a small chat app a single queue (or even direct database writes) would be simpler.

decisions.why: Conversations need ordering, pagination and search with strong consistency; a relational store with indexes handles this well at moderate scale.
decisions.tradeoff: Very high write volume eventually requires partitioning by conversation or moving hot history to a wide-column store.

versions.title: Single server
versions.summary: One server holds all WebSockets and writes straight to the database. Works until one process cannot hold every connection.

versions.title: Many servers + Redis
versions.summary: A load balancer spreads connections; Redis Pub/Sub lets servers exchange messages so users on different servers can talk.

versions.title: Event log
versions.summary: Kafka records every message as an event; persistence moves off the hot path into a consumer.

versions.title: More consumers
versions.summary: Notifications and analytics consume the same stream without touching the chat servers.

textAlternative: Browsers connect over WebSocket to a load balancer, which distributes connections across two chat servers. Both chat servers publish and subscribe to Redis so a message received on one server reaches recipients connected to the other. Messages are also written as events to Kafka. Three consumers read from Kafka: a message service that stores history in PostgreSQL, a notification service that pushes to offline users, and an analytics service.
